1.1

Preliminaries and Definitions for the Point Star Unfolding

Definition 1 Let PPP be a convex polyhedron, and let xxx be a point on PPP. The star unfolding, SxS_{x}Sx​, is a 2-dimensional polygon formed by cutting PPP along a shortest path from every vertex of PPP to xxx, and flattening the result into the plane. See Fig. 2. Note that there is a choice of cuts if a vertex has more than one shortest path to xxx.

DefinitionsComplete componentPaper: partial coverage+

Formalization
Definitions present for cofacial cuts

Scope of this correspondence: Straight source-to-vertex cuts on a convex polyhedron. Their interpretation as shortest surface cuts uses a source sharing a face with every vertex.

Explanation, scope and remaining work

ConvexPolyhedron is the convex hull of its exact extreme vertices in ℝ³, with nonempty interior. The current starCuts removes straight source-to-vertex segments. These are shortest surface cuts when the source is cofacial with every vertex. This is not yet a definition of an arbitrary choice of shortest cuts for an arbitrary source.

Beyond this milestone — not claimed complete
  • Chosen shortest cuts for arbitrary sources, and their general cut surface, remain an extension beyond this milestone.

If PPP has nnn vertices, then the polygon SxS_{x}Sx​ will have 2n2n2n vertices in general, and 2(n−1)2(n - 1)2(n−1) vertices if xxx is located at a vertex of PPP. The vertices of SxS_{x}Sx​ alternate around the boundary between vertex images, denoted viv_{i}vi​, that correspond to the vertices of PPP, and nnn ‘copies’ of xxx, called source images and denoted by xix_{i}xi​. See Fig. 2. The edges of SxS_{x}Sx​ correspond to the shortest path cuts made from each vertex to xxx. Therefore, the two edges incident to any vertex image viv_{i}vi​ are always the same length.

The cut locus (or “ridge tree”), TxT_{x}Tx​, is the closure of the set of all points on the surface of PPP that have more than one shortest path to xxx. It is known that the cut locus is a tree [12], and that its edges are shortest paths [1] and thus correspond to straight-line segments in SxS_{x}Sx​. See Fig. 2b. As a corollary to their proof of non-overlap [3, Thm. 10.2], Aronov and O’Rourke proved that the cut locus is a subset of the Voronoi diagram of the images of xxx, but we will not use this result.

Scope of this correspondence: At most six vertices; every face triangular or quadrilateral. Arbitrary surface source.

Explanation, scope and remaining work

The new theorem constructs an exact finite embedded tree, not a graph covering a superset. Its definition augments the multiple-route locus by the nonsource original vertices. Equality with the paper’s closure definition has a checked canonical-graph theorem; that equality is not yet exported in the broader small-polyhedron scope.

How the proof is split

  1. Exact local Voronoi descriptions → finite straight segments.
  2. Continuous retraction onto the cut set → contractibility → connectedness and acyclicity.
  3. Mark original cut vertices and all junctions → exactly two shortest routes on an open tree edge.

1.2

Preliminaries and Definitions for the Geodesic Star Unfolding

Lean annotation: included for completeness; curve-source unfolding is outside this point-star formalization. Continue to the point proof →

Given a polyhedron PPP, a geodesic curve λ\lambdaλ on PPP is a curve on the surface of PPP, such that at every interior point ppp of λ\lambdaλ, the surface angle to either side of ppp is exactly π\piπ. If the surface angle to either side of ppp is at most π\piπ then the curve is called a quasigeodesic. We will only consider [quasi]geodesic curves that are simple, meaning there is no point of self-intersection between any two interior (i.e., non-endpoint) points of the curve.

The endpoints of λ\lambdaλ are labelled aaa and bbb and the two sides of λ\lambdaλ are labelled sss and ttt, with the convention that the clockwise order around λ\lambdaλ on the outside surface of PPP is a,s,b,ta, s, b, ta,s,b,t. We distinguish shortest paths to λ\lambdaλ that arrive at (or “report to”) aaa or bbb, and shortest paths that arrive at interior points of λ\lambdaλ on side sss or ttt. Any shortest path that arrives at an interior point of λ\lambdaλ forms a right angle with λ\lambdaλ, as shown by the following lemma, which is a special case of [9, Lem. 1].

In the unfolding SλS_{\lambda}Sλ​, a source image is either a copy of an endpoint (aaa or bbb), called a point image, or a sub-segment of λ\lambdaλ corresponding to side sss or ttt, called a segment image. (Note that a segment image might include one of the endpoints of λ\lambdaλ.) Around a clockwise traversal of the boundary of SλS_{\lambda}Sλ​ we encounter source images in order a,s,b,ta, s, b, ta,s,b,t—this is because our convention is to draw the inside of the polyhedron’s surface facing up. Each consecutive pair of source images is separated by two edges of equal length joined at a vertex image, such that the edges correspond to the shortest path cut at the vertex.

The cut locus of a geodesic λ\lambdaλ, denoted TλT_{\lambda}Tλ​, is the closure of the set of all points on the surface of PPP that have more than one shortest path to λ\lambdaλ. The cut locus of a geodesic is a tree [13]. (An alternate proof can be found in [4, Lem. 4]. The lemma applies to the outside of any closed convex curve on the surface of PPP—in the present situation, the closed convex curve is the set of points at some fixed distance ε\varepsilonε from λ\lambdaλ.) See ahead to Fig. 6.

A key difference from the point case is that the edges of the geodesic cut locus are not necessarily straight-line segments. Every edge of the cut locus is the locus of points that are equidistant from two source images. Thus, when the two sources to either side of an edge are a point image and a segment image respectively, a parabolic cut locus edge will result. The cut locus edges between pairs of point images or pairs of segment images will still be straight.

2

New Proof for the Point Star Unfolding

In this section we give a new proof of non-overlap for the point star unfolding that is simpler than the original proof of Aronov and O’Rourke [3].

The most important idea of our proof is to partition the star unfolding into pairs of congruent triangles. Each vertex of the cut locus has three or more shortest paths to xxx on the surface of PPP. Add all these shortest paths as line segments in the star unfolding. We use the following basic properties of shortest paths: (1) no two shortest paths to xxx (or more generally, to a geodesic curve) cross each other [9, Lem. 2] (their lemma is stated for vertices of the polyhedron, but applies more generally); and (2) no shortest path crosses the cut locus [12, Lem. 4.2]. These properties imply that when we add the line segments corresponding to shortest paths between xxx and cut locus vertices, each edge of the cut locus will have a triangle to each side. Because all shortest paths from a cut locus vertex to the nearest source images have the same length, the two triangles to either side of a cut locus edge have corresponding sides of equal length, and therefore are congruent. We call each such pair of triangles a kite. The kite associated with cut locus edge eee is denoted kite⁡(e)\operatorname{kite}(e)kite(e). The two images of xxx to each side of eee are called the apex vertices of the kite. Observe that the kites form a partition of SxS_{x}Sx​. See Fig. 2b.

Both actual radial triangles, their coverage of the surface, and coherent charts now have small-polyhedron proofs without a canonical graph assumption. The chart construction proves the original-vertex leaf condition and flat-junction compatibility; later separation handles overlap.

How the proof is split

  1. No branching/crossing of distinct shortest routes.
  2. Proper shortest prefixes stay outside the cut set.
  3. Construct both actual closed radial strips and develop them to metric triangles.
  4. Prove their union covers the surface; later separation handles overlap.

Explanation, scope and remaining work

The proof covers each original vertex cone by its actual incident radial triangles, accounts for the flat junctions and tree angles, and proves a sufficient total-curvature bound from the original faces. It yields a directed source-angle sum bounded by the source surface angle. Since that angle is <2π<2\pi<2π, the half-sum is <π<\pi<π. No canonical graph assumption is needed.

How the proof is split

  1. Local surface angle <2π<2\pi<2π: checked for all small polyhedra.

  4. Tree angle accounting gives half the directed source-angle sum <π<\pi<π.

Explanation, scope and remaining work

universal_star_embedding constructs a continuous open embedding of the actual retained surface into the plane, with bounded path-connected image, finite straight-segment boundary, and exact local intrinsic isometry. The tree, charts, angle budget and separation are all proved from the solid. The displayed whole-face consequence also covers at most six vertices with a universal vertex, using the earlier reductions. Neither result claims the paper’s theorem for arbitrary sources and unrestricted polyhedra.

  2. Prove the angle budget and separate every pair of kites.

  4. Prove local intrinsic isometry and retained-surface connectivity.
  5. Identify the exact finite-segment boundary.

Let ki=kite⁡(ei)k_{i} = \operatorname{kite}(e_{i})ki​=kite(ei​). We will show that k1k_{1}k1​ and ktk_{t}kt​ have disjoint interiors. We will define a sequence of regions W1,…,Wt−1W_{1}, \ldots, W_{t-1}W1​,…,Wt−1​, called WWW-wedges, so that WiW_{i}Wi​ includes k1,…,kik_{1}, \ldots, k_{i}k1​,…,ki​ and excludes ki+1k_{i+1}ki+1​. Then Wt−1W_{t-1}Wt−1​ includes k1k_{1}k1​ and excludes ktk_{t}kt​, which will complete the proof.

The boundary of the WWW-wedge WiW_{i}Wi​ consists of four edges, generally shaped like a ‘WWW’ and defined as follows. The center point of WiW_{i}Wi​ is the point pip_{i}pi​, where eie_{i}ei​ and ei+1e_{i+1}ei+1​ intersect; the inner legs are the edges of kik_{i}ki​ that are incident to pip_{i}pi​; and the outer legs form an angle with the inner legs (on the side of kik_{i}ki​) of π2+αi\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha _{i}2π​+αi​, where αi=∑j=1iα(ej)\alpha _{i} = \sum_{j=1}^{i} \alpha (e_{j})αi​=∑j=1i​α(ej​). The outer legs extend either to their point of intersection, or as infinite rays if they do not intersect. This boundary divides the plane into two regions and we define WiW_{i}Wi​ to be the region containing kik_{i}ki​ in a neighbourhood of pip_{i}pi​. We also define W0W_{0}W0​ to have center point p0p_{0}p0​, with inner legs along the edges of k1k_{1}k1​ and outer legs rotated outward (on the opposite side from k1k_{1}k1​) by π2\frac{\pi}{2}2π​. See Fig. 4. Note that αi\alpha _{i}αi​ is in the range [0,π][0, \pi ][0,π] as observed above.

Scope of this correspondence: Planar kites and wedges; coordinate formulations of the paper’s geometric step.

Explanation, scope and remaining work

The code does not reproduce the circular-sector proof line by line. It proves kite containment and complementary exclusion by coordinate inequalities, then translates the angle budget to these inequalities in rotate_and_move. The full geometric step bundles rotation, exclusion and root movement.

How the proof is split

  1. Containment: a nonnegative dot product keeps the outer ray pointing outward.
  2. Exclusion: the outward condition at the new root keeps the next kite outside the old wedge.
  3. Angle-to-coordinate translation connects these conditions to the cumulative budget.

The Lean induction tracks three facts separately: the old wedge is contained in an enlarged wedge, the enlarged wedge avoids the next kite’s interior, and moving coordinates turns their union into the new wedge. It explicitly transports every kite into one common plane.

  3. updated: WiW_iWi​ is the transported union Wi′∪kiW_i^{\prime}\cup k_iWi′​∪ki​.
  4. Finite induction carries all earlier regions forward and separates the endpoints.

Note that the unfolding does not overlap in the neighbourhood of point pip_{i}pi​—this is true whether pip_{i}pi​ is a point with 2π2\pi2π surface area, or a vertex, which will be incident to a single cut. Thus the kites kik_{i}ki​ and ki−1k_{i-1}ki−1​, which are both incident to pip_{i}pi​, do not overlap. Rotate each of the inner legs of Wi−1W_{i-1}Wi−1​ about point pi−1p_{i-1}pi−1​, away from ki−1k_{i-1}ki−1​ to the edge of kik_{i}ki​. This is a rotation by 0∘0^{\circ}0∘ when an edge of ki−1k_{i-1}ki−1​ is coincident with an edge of kik_{i}ki​. Keep the angle between inner and outer legs fixed throughout the rotation. Observe that all the kite edges incident to pi−1p_{i-1}pi−1​ have the same length, so we really perform a rigid transformation on each half of the WWW. Call the resulting WWW-wedge Wi′W^{\prime}_{i}Wi′​ (shown as a dashed poly-line in Fig. 4). Notice that Wi′W^{\prime}_{i}Wi′​ contains Wi−1W_{i-1}Wi−1​, because the angle αi−1+π2\alpha _{i-1} + \frac{\pi}{2}αi−1​+2π​ is in the range [π2,3π2][\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}][2π​,23π​] so the outer legs remain outside the rotation sector of the inner legs. (Here it is crucial that we added the extra π2\frac{\pi}{2}2π​ to the initial angle.) That kik_{i}ki​ is outside Wi′W^{\prime}_{i}Wi′​ follows from applying Lemma 2 to the outside of Wi′W^{\prime}_{i}Wi′​, noting that αi−1+α(ei)≤π\alpha _{i-1} + \alpha (e_{i}) \le \piαi−1​+α(ei​)≤π so the angle αi−1+π2\alpha _{i-1} + \frac{\pi}{2}αi−1​+2π​ is in the range [π2,3π2−α(ei)][\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2} - \alpha (e_{i})][2π​,23π​−α(ei​)] and therefore the complementary angle is in the range [α(ei)+π2,3π2][\alpha (e_{i}) + \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}][α(ei​)+2π​,23π​].

Our proof, like Aronov and O’Rourke’s, shows a stronger result that certain regions outside the star unfolding are empty. Aronov and O’Rourke [3] showed that at any vertex viv_{i}vi​ adjacent to source images xix_{i}xi​ and xi+1x_{i+1}xi+1​ in the unfolding, no part of the unfolding enters the circular sector centered at viv_{i}vi​ exterior to the unfolding near viv_{i}vi​ and bounded by the radii vixiv_{i} x_{i}vi​xi​ and vixi+1v_{i} x_{i+1}vi​xi+1​. See Fig. 5. Our proof shows that larger regions are empty, as formalized in the following lemma.

Proof In non-degenerate situations, viv_{i}vi​ is a leaf of the cut locus. Let eee be the cut locus edge incident to viv_{i}vi​. For any kite k=kite⁡(f)k = \operatorname{kite}(f)k=kite(f) of the unfolding, consider the path in the cut locus starting with eee and ending with fff, and apply the above proof to this path. Wedge WWW in the statement of the lemma is wedge W0W_{0}W0​ in the proof, and the proof shows that kite kkk does not enter wedge W0W_{0}W0​.

Explanation, scope and remaining work

Every original cut-tree vertex is proved to be a leaf for a cofacial source. Thus a path through two different tree edges cannot have an original polyhedron vertex as its internal junction. This supplies exactly the leaf condition needed by the completed universal-source charts. The exact closed-unfolding-versus-interior-of-WWW assertion of Lemma 3 remains additional paper correspondence.

More generally, viv_{i}vi​ may be an internal vertex of the cut locus with more than one incident cut locus edge, and we need a slight generalization of this argument. Consider any kite k=kite⁡(f)k = \operatorname{kite}(f)k=kite(f) of the unfolding, and consider the path in the cut locus starting with viv_{i}vi​ and ending with fff. Apply the above proof to this path. The path will use one of the cut locus edges incident to viv_{i}vi​. The crucial observation is that wedge WWW in the statement of the lemma is a subset of wedge W0W_{0}W0​ in the proof for this path. The proof shows that kite kkk does not enter wedge W0W_{0}W0​, and therefore kkk does not enter WWW. □
